questions.q: On a physical map, a traveller going inland from the coast crosses these colours in turn: blue, green, light yellow, dark brown. Which description fits the chapter's colour code?
questions.a: A water body, then plains, then a desert, then high mountains beyond
o: A water body, then plains, then a desert, then high mountains beyond
A water body, then a plateau, then a desert, then a line of high mountains
A water body, then plains, then a plateau, then ice and glaciers
A water body, then plains, then a desert, then ice and glaciers

questions.q: The chapter says, 'Every map is a compromise.' Explain what is being compromised, using both projections the chapter gives.
questions.a: A flat map cannot keep both shape and size right. The Mercator Projection keeps shape and direction but greatly distorts size near the poles, so its compromise favours navigation. The Robinson Projection balances size and shape distortions, so neither is exact.
s: What is traded off: shape against size
Mercator: shape and direction kept, size distorted near poles
Robinson: balances both, so neither is exact

questions.q:
Read the statements about maps and projections.
1. A cartographer who draws the right shape of every country can also be sure of showing each country at its right size.
2. The Mercator Projection preserves direction, and the chapter says this makes it useful for navigation.
3. On a physical map, light yellow stands for deserts and white stands for ice and glaciers.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
All three: 1, 2 and 3
2 only
1 only

questions.q: A school library wants one wall map of the world for students to browse. The librarian asks for a map in which neither shapes nor sizes are badly off, even if it is not the best for plotting a ship's course. Which choice fits the chapter?
questions.a: The Robinson Projection, a compromise balancing size and shape distortions across the map
o: The Robinson Projection, a compromise balancing size and shape distortions across the map
The Mercator Projection, since it preserves shape and direction and so leaves no size error
The Robinson Projection, since it removes distortion altogether and is exact
The Mercator Projection, since it is the only one that shows true sizes near the poles

questions.q: A friend says: 'The Robinson map looks more realistic, so it must be accurate everywhere.' Give the chapter's correction in two points.
questions.a: The Robinson Projection is a compromise that balances size and shape distortions, so it is not exact; and every map has some distortion, so none is accurate everywhere.
s: It is a compromise balancing size and shape distortions
Every map has some distortion

questions.q: Anita says: 'The Robinson Projection removes distortion. It also gives a more visually pleasing, realistic map.' Test each sentence against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The second sentence is right: the chapter calls the Robinson map visually pleasing and realistic. The first is wrong: it is a compromise that balances size and shape distortions, and every map has some distortion.
s: Second sentence correct
First sentence wrong: it balances distortion, it does not remove it
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: Two students each measure the same island on a different wall map and get different sizes. Each says the other's map must be faulty. Which view agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Neither need be faulty: projections distort differently, so two honest maps can give different sizes
o: Neither need be faulty: projections distort differently, so two honest maps can give different sizes
One of the maps must be faulty, because a correct projection would give the same size in every map
The larger measurement is the true one, since a map can only make a landmass look smaller than it is
Both are faulty, because a flat map of the Earth cannot be used to compare sizes of any kind

questions.q: Ria peels an orange in one piece and presses the peel flat on her desk. It tears, however carefully she works. Her teacher says this models the work of a cartographer. Which conclusion does the chapter draw from this test?
questions.a: Showing a nearly round Earth on a flat surface must distort it somewhere, so every map has some distortion
o: Showing a nearly round Earth on a flat surface must distort it somewhere, so every map has some distortion
Cartographers have not yet tried enough methods, so a flat map without distortion will come in time
The tearing shows that only hand-drawn maps are distorted and printed maps are exact
The Earth is perfectly round, so a peel done properly should have lain flat

questions.q: A school must choose maps for two uses: a chart for the model-ship club, which cares about direction, and a wall map for the general corridor. (a) Recommend a projection for each, with the chapter's reason. (b) Name the weakness of the club's chart that students must be warned about. (c) Say what the club should also keep to find an exact position.
questions.a: (a) The Mercator Projection for the model-ship club, because it preserves shape and direction and is useful for navigation; the Robinson Projection for the corridor, because it balances size and shape distortions and gives a pleasing realistic map. (b) The Mercator greatly distorts size near the poles, so Greenland looks as big as Africa. (c) Latitude and longitude coordinates, which professionals use because they are more precise.
s: Mercator for the club with reason
Robinson for the corridor with reason
Warning: size greatly distorted near the poles
Example of the distortion (Greenland as big as Africa)
Coordinates for exact positions

questions.q:
(a) A cartographer's flat map shows every country's shape exactly right. According to the chapter, what may be wrong with it?
(b) Using (a), say which of the chapter's two projections fits this description and what it is useful for.
questions.a: (a) Some maps show the right shapes of countries but the wrong sizes, so the sizes may be wrong. (b) The Mercator Projection, which preserves shape and direction and is useful for navigation.
s: (a) Right shapes can come with wrong sizes
(b) Mercator, useful for navigation

questions.q: A club hangs a Mercator map and a Robinson map side by side. Rahul says, 'One of them must be wrong, because Africa looks different on the two.' Give two reasons why differences between projections are expected.
questions.a: Each projection uses a different method to draw the world, and every map is a compromise: some show the right shapes but wrong sizes, others the right sizes but distorted shapes. So two maps can differ without either being wrong.
s: Different methods are used to draw the world
Every map is a compromise between shape and size

questions.q: A ship's navigator needs a world map that preserves shape and direction, which the chapter says makes a projection useful for navigation. She asks for the ___ Projection.
questions.a: Mercator

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the Mercator Projection preserves shape and direction, every country on it also appears at its true size.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The Mercator Projection preserves shape and direction, but the chapter says it greatly distorts size near the poles, which is why Greenland looks as big as Africa.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: shape and direction kept, but size greatly distorted near the poles

questions.q: A principal wants a single poster that tells Class 8 students why they should not trust one map alone. Write the poster's slogan and the one reason from the chapter that backs it.
questions.a: For example: 'Every map is a compromise, so look at many.' The reason is that some projections show right shapes but wrong sizes while others show right sizes but distorted shapes, so only several projections together give a fair understanding.
s: A slogan that says every map is a compromise or a call to use many projections
The reason: shapes and sizes cannot both be right on a flat map

questions.q: A surveyor is asked for the precise position of a proposed bridge site. A trainee suggests reading it off a Mercator wall map because it preserves shape and direction. What should the surveyor reply, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Professionals use latitude and longitude coordinates, which are more precise
o: Professionals use latitude and longitude coordinates, which are more precise
A Mercator map is precise everywhere, so reading the wall map is enough for the surveyor
A Robinson map must be used instead, because it is the one professionals rely on for positions
Coordinates are only for the poles, where the Mercator is unreliable, so use the wall map elsewhere

questions.q:
Assertion (A): No flat map of the Earth can be free of distortion.
Reason (R): A map projection can preserve shape, size, direction and distance all at once.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A map-making class colours a physical map of an imaginary continent using the chapter's colour code. From south to north it has a band of blue, a wide band of green, a belt of yellow/brown, a narrow belt of dark brown and, at the far north, patches of white. In the west lies a patch of light yellow.
(a) State what each colour shows, in order from south to north, and for the western patch.
(b) A student says the yellow/brown belt must be a mountain range because it is higher than the green band. Use the chapter's definitions to correct her.
(c) Which band would you expect to carry the densest farming, and what does the chapter say about why?
(d) The class adds a large dry region and asks what colour the code gives a desert. Name it, and say what a reader still cannot tell from that colour alone.
questions.a: (a) Blue: water bodies; green: plains; yellow/brown: plateau; dark brown: high mountains; white: ice and glaciers; light yellow: desert. (b) A plateau rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, while mountains have a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit; being higher than the plains does not make it a mountain. (c) The green plains: the chapter says plains have fertile soils that support farming and dense populations. (d) Light yellow; the colour does not show whether the desert is hot or cold, since the chapter names both hot and cold deserts.
s: Part (a): six colour meanings
Part (b): plateau flat surface versus mountain narrow summit
Part (c): plains, fertile soils support farming
Part (d): light yellow; hot or cold is not shown

questions.q:
A school can buy only one world map for its corridor, and the geography teacher wants it to help Class 8 students compare how big different countries really are. She narrows the choice to a Mercator map and a Robinson map. The Mercator map preserves shape and direction and is useful for navigation. The Robinson map is a compromise that balances size and shape distortions.
(a) What does the Mercator map greatly distort, and where?
(b) Give one example from the chapter of the effect of that distortion.
(c) Which map should the school buy for the teacher's purpose, and why?
(d) Name one use for which your choice would be a poorer map, and say what the school should keep for exact positions.
questions.a: (a) It greatly distorts size near the poles. (b) Greenland looks larger than India on it, though Greenland is smaller (it also looks as big as Africa). (c) The Robinson map, because it balances size and shape distortions so sizes are less badly off for comparing countries. (d) It is poorer for navigation, where the Mercator preserves direction; for exact positions use latitude and longitude coordinates, which professionals use as they are more precise.
s: Part (a): size, near the poles
Part (b): Greenland looks larger than India
Part (c): Robinson, balanced size and shape
Part (d): poorer for navigation; use coordinates for exact positions

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'To understand the world fairly, we must look at multiple projections, not just one.' Use the orange-peel test, the Greenland example and the two projections of the chapter.
questions.a: The orange peel cannot be laid flat without tearing, so every flat map of the oblate spheroid Earth has some distortion. Because of this, some maps keep shapes but get sizes wrong and others keep sizes but distort shapes. The Mercator keeps shape and direction but makes Greenland look as big as Africa and larger than India, though it is smaller. The Robinson balances the two distortions but is also a compromise. Since none is free of distortion, only several together give a fair picture.
s: Orange test: all maps distort
Maps trade shape against size
Greenland example from the Mercator
Robinson as another compromise
Conclusion: use several projections for a fair view

questions.q: Write a short situation in which relying on one projection alone leads a person to a wrong conclusion, and say what the person should have done instead.
questions.a: For example: a student looks only at a Mercator map where Greenland looks larger than India and concludes Greenland is the bigger country. In fact Greenland is smaller. She should have looked at more than one projection, since every map is a compromise.
s: A situation in which one map misleads about size or shape
The wrong conclusion drawn from the distortion
The remedy: compare multiple projections

questions.q: A student draws the Earth's surface as 200 equal squares and colours the ocean's share blue using the chapter's figure. The number of squares left uncoloured is ___.

(a) Name two ways in which the oceans help regulate the climate.
(b) Using (a), explain how a coastal town's rainfall can be linked to the ocean.
questions.a: (a) They absorb heat and slowly release it, and they add moisture to the air. (b) The moisture added to the air forms clouds and rainfall, so the ocean beside the town is a source of its rain.
s: (a) Absorbing and slowly releasing heat; adding moisture to the air
(b) Moisture forms clouds and rainfall

questions.q:
Premise from the chapter's Fig. 1.5: the Arctic Ocean is labelled 'smallest, shallowest, covered with sea ice, home to polar bears and walruses', and the Southern Ocean is labelled 'encircles Antarctica; penguins and seals'. A ship's crew sights polar bears on sea ice. A second crew meets penguins and seals while sailing round Antarctica.
(a) Name the ocean each crew is in.
(b) Say which of the two oceans is the smaller and shallower.
questions.a: (a) The first crew is in the Arctic Ocean and the second in the Southern Ocean. (b) The Arctic Ocean is the smaller and shallower.
s: (a) Southern Ocean; Arctic Ocean
(b) The Arctic Ocean is smaller and shallower

questions.q: A student claims, 'Nothing can live in the Mariana Trench.' Name two conditions she would cite, and the chapter's evidence against her.
questions.a: She would cite near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness. But scientists have found unique life forms there; with no light, they use energy from chemicals in the water to produce food.
s: Two harsh conditions: near-freezing, high pressure or darkness
Evidence: unique life forms using chemical energy

questions.q:
A teacher in Surat makes a paper model of the Earth's surface of 500 square centimetres (an illustrative size) and paints the ocean's share blue. She also puts 100 beads in a jar to stand for all the Earth's water, and sets aside a bowl for the ocean's beads.
(a) Using the chapter's figure for the share of the surface covered by the ocean, how many square centimetres does she paint blue, and how many stay unpainted?
(b) Using the chapter's figure for the share of water held by the oceans, how many beads belong in the ocean bowl?
(c) A student says the bowl should hold 71 beads, because the paper is 71 per cent blue. Another says 97. Decide who is right and why.
(d) Which of the two models, the painted paper or the bead bowl, shows the ocean's share of the Earth's water?
questions.a: (a) 71 per cent of 500 = 355 square centimetres blue; 145 stay unpainted. (b) 97 per cent of 100 = 97 beads. (c) The second student: 71 per cent is the share of the surface the ocean covers, while the oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water. (d) The bead bowl, because the painted paper shows surface cover, not water.
s: Part (a): 355 and 145 square centimetres
Part (b): 97 beads
Part (c): 97, since 71 per cent is the surface share
Part (d): the bead bowl shows the water share

questions.q: A student writes in her notebook: 'The ocean covers about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface, so it holds about 71 per cent of the Earth's water.' Which correction is right according to the chapter?
questions.a: The 71 per cent is its share of the surface; the oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water
o: The 71 per cent is its share of the surface; the oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water
Both figures are shares of the surface, and the water share is not given anywhere
The oceans hold 71 per cent of the water, and the 97 per cent is the share of surface they cover
The oceans hold 97 per cent of the surface and 71 per cent of the water, so her figures are swapped

questions.q: Compare how food is made in the sunlit ocean and in the Mariana Trench: the conditions in the trench, the energy source in each, who makes the food, and what the two have in common.
questions.a: In the sunlit ocean plankton, which have chlorophyll, use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make food. The Mariana Trench has near-freezing temperatures, high pressure and complete darkness, so plants cannot photosynthesise there; life uses energy from chemicals in the water to produce food, and a snail photographed there feeds on bacteria that synthesise chemicals for their own food. What they have in common is that in both places living things make their own food, one using sunlight and the other chemical energy.
s: Trench conditions: near-freezing, high pressure, darkness
Sunlit ocean: plankton, sunlight and carbon dioxide
Trench: energy from chemicals, no photosynthesis
Trench snail feeds on bacteria that synthesise chemicals
Common point: both make their own food, one from sunlight and one from chemical energy

questions.q:
Two coastal towns lie at the same latitude. A water-temperature log shows that in winter the sea at Town P is much warmer than at Town Q. A local scientist notes that a current brings water to P from near the Equator across an ocean, while a current brings water to Q from a polar region.
(a) Say whether the current at P and the current at Q is warm or cold.
(b) Name the real current of the chapter that behaves like the one at P, and the effect it has on a European country.
(c) A student says, 'Two towns at the same latitude must have the same climate.' Use the log and the chapter to show what is wrong.
(d) Predict how Q's sea would change if its current were replaced by one from near the Equator, and give the chapter fact your prediction rests on.
questions.a: (a) P: warm current; Q: cold current. (b) The Gulf Stream, which flows north from near the Equator through the Atlantic toward Western Europe and makes the United Kingdom warmer than other places at the same latitude. (c) The chapter says currents affect the climate of coastal areas, so two places at one latitude can differ, as P and Q do. (d) Q's water would be warmer, because warm currents bring warm water from the equator and currents affect the climate of coastal areas.
s: Part (a): warm at P, cold at Q
Part (b): Gulf Stream; warms the UK relative to its latitude
Part (c): currents change coastal climate at one latitude
Part (d): warmer, since warm currents bring warm water and affect coastal climate

questions.q: A pollutant in a bay kills a large mass of plankton along the coast. A student predicts the effect from the chapter. Which prediction is the best supported?
questions.a: Less food and oxygen are made, and the oceans' share of nearly half our oxygen falls
o: Less food and oxygen are made, and the oceans' share of nearly half our oxygen falls
Nothing changes in the air we breathe, as land plants alone give all of the oxygen
Only blue whales are affected, since they are the one animal that eats plankton at all
The oceans would stop absorbing heat, because plankton are what hold the heat

questions.q: Dev says: 'The Gulf Stream carries cold water from the poles toward the Equator, so places along it are colder than other places at their latitude.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The Gulf Stream flows north from near the Equator, where the water is warm, through the Atlantic towards Western Europe. It is a warm current and makes places like the United Kingdom warmer, not colder, than other places at the same latitude.
s: It starts near the Equator where water is warm
It is warm and makes the UK warmer than places at its latitude
Verdict: no

questions.q: Premise from the chapter's Fig. 1.5: the Southern Ocean 'encircles Antarctica; penguins and seals', and the Arctic Ocean is 'covered with sea ice, home to polar bears and walruses'. Write a riddle of two clues whose answer is the Southern Ocean. Give the answer and say which clue is the more useful in telling it from the Arctic Ocean.
questions.a: For example: 'I encircle Antarctica. Penguins and seals live in me.' The answer is the Southern Ocean. The first clue is more useful, since the Arctic Ocean is the one with sea ice, polar bears and walruses, so a clue about those would point to it.
s: Two correct clues
The answer: Southern Ocean
Which clue separates it from the Arctic Ocean

questions.q: True or False? 'Because plankton are microscopic, their loss would matter only to sea animals and not to people living on land.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The oceans give us almost half the oxygen we breathe, and tiny marine organisms like plankton make this possible, so harm to them would affect land animals and people too.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: plankton help supply almost half of the oxygen we breathe

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Pollution that harms the ocean is a problem even for people who live far from the sea.' Use plankton and oxygen, the climate roles of the ocean, and the chapter's two figures about the ocean.
questions.a: Plankton, which have chlorophyll and use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make food, help the oceans give us almost half the oxygen we breathe; if pollution harmed them, people anywhere would have less oxygen. The oceans also regulate the climate by absorbing heat, slowly releasing it and adding moisture that forms clouds and rainfall, which reaches inland as well as coastal areas. They cover about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface and hold 97 per cent of its water, so harming them touches most of the planet.
s: Plankton and almost half of our oxygen
Pollution harming plankton reduces oxygen for people everywhere
Climate roles: heat absorbed and released slowly
Moisture forms clouds and rainfall
71 per cent of the surface and 97 per cent of the water

questions.q: A research robot is lowered to the Challenger Deep, where it is near-freezing, under great pressure and completely dark. It films a snail feeding on bacteria. Which explanation fits the chapter for how food is made there?
questions.a: The bacteria make food from chemical energy in the water, as no light reaches
o: The bacteria make food from chemical energy in the water, as no light reaches
The bacteria make food using sunlight that slowly reaches the trench floor through the water
The snail makes its own food by photosynthesis, using the chlorophyll in its shell
No food is made at all, and the snail survives by eating plankton sinking from above in the dark

questions.q: A student says the ocean floor must be as flat as a swimming pool, so a camera dragged along it would see only smooth ground. (a) Name two features the chapter says you would also expect to find. (b) Say what on land they resemble.
questions.a: (a) Mountains and valleys (and plains). (b) The chapter says the ocean floor has mountains, valleys and plains like the land.
s: (a) Mountains, valleys and plains on the ocean floor
(b) They resemble the landforms on land

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The oceans help regulate the climate.
Reason (R): The ocean floor has mountains, valleys and plains like the land.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Show that plants making food by photosynthesis cannot be the food-makers in the Challenger Deep, using the chapter.
questions.a: Plants and plankton use sunlight, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll to make food. The Mariana Trench is in complete darkness, so no light is available for photosynthesis; the chapter says life there uses energy from chemicals in the water instead.
s: Photosynthesis needs sunlight
The trench is in complete darkness
Life there uses chemical energy instead

questions.q: A town beside the sea stays warm for hours after sunset on a hot day, and clouds keep forming over the water. Which two roles of the oceans does the chapter give that match these observations?
questions.a: Slowly releasing heat the water absorbed, and adding moisture to the air that forms clouds and rainfall
o: Slowly releasing heat the water absorbed, and adding moisture to the air that forms clouds and rainfall
Absorbing all heat so that the town never gets warm, and removing moisture from the air
Producing almost half of the oxygen we breathe, and carrying warm currents toward the poles
Holding 97 per cent of the Earth's water, and covering about 71 per cent of the surface

questions.q:
Premise from the chapter's Fig. 1.5: the Arctic Ocean is labelled 'smallest, shallowest, covered with sea ice, home to polar bears and walruses' and the Pacific Ocean 'the largest and deepest; whales, tuna'. Match each observation in Column A with the term in Column B that the chapter would use.
Column A: 1. Water moves from near the Equator through the Atlantic toward Western Europe.  2. The smallest, shallowest ocean, covered with sea ice, where walruses live.  3. A deep V-shaped area of the seafloor with near-freezing water, high pressure and darkness.  4. The largest and deepest ocean, with whales and tuna.
Column B: a. the Gulf Stream, a warm current  b. the Arctic Ocean  c. a trench  d. the Pacific Ocean

Read the statements about the ocean floor and its trenches.
1. The seafloor has very deep, V-shaped areas called trenches.
2. The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench, and its shallowest section is called the Challenger Deep.
3. The oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
All three: 1, 2 and 3
1 only
2 only

questions.q:
(a) State one reason the chapter gives for the importance of the Persian Gulf.
(b) State one reason it gives for the importance of bays in general.
questions.a: (a) The Persian Gulf has been important for trade between India and Europe for millennia. (b) Bays provide safe havens for ports and dockyards, shielding them from the strong winds of the open oceans.
s: (a) Trade between India and Europe for millennia
(b) Safe havens for ports and dockyards sheltered from strong winds

questions.q: A port authority lists four water bodies. P is a man-made channel connecting the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. Q is a narrow channel joining two seas. R is a smaller, broad inlet of the sea. S is a large inlet deeply cutting into land. Which naming matches the chapter's classification?
questions.a: P is a canal, Q is a strait, R is a bay and S is a gulf
o: P is a canal, Q is a strait, R is a bay and S is a gulf
P is a strait, Q is a canal, R is a gulf and S is a bay
P is a canal, Q is a strait, R is a gulf and S is a bay
P is a canal, Q is a sea, R is a bay and S is a strait

questions.q: A diver reports a long ridge of bare rock just below the surface of the ocean, with no coral growing on it. A friend says, 'Then it is not a reef, because reefs are made only by corals.' Going by the chapter, which statement is right?
questions.a: It can still be a reef, since a reef is a ridge at or near the surface of the ocean and natural reefs may be made of rock
o: It can still be a reef, since a reef is a ridge at or near the surface of the ocean and natural reefs may be made of rock
It is not a reef, because a reef must always be built by tiny sea animals called corals
It is a reef only if humans built it, since natural ridges are not counted as reefs at all
It is a reef only if it shelters one-quarter of all ocean species in the same place

questions.q: A survey boat inspects the Great Barrier Reef along its whole length, covering 40 km a day. Using the chapter's length for the reef, the survey takes ___ days.
A tourism notice near a reef says: 'Coral bleaching is just nature's cycle, so tourists need not worry.' Which response best fits the chapter?
questions.a: It follows changes in ocean water chemistry, largely caused by human actions, and costs animals their habitat
o: It follows changes in ocean water chemistry, largely caused by human actions, and costs animals their habitat
It is harmless, because the death of the coral never affects the many sea animals that live and feed in the reef
It is caused by overfishing alone, since fish are what keep the colour of the coral on the reef
It is natural, but only on reefs that humans have built artificially and not on natural ones

questions.q:
Read the statements about reefs and water bodies.
1. All natural reefs are built by corals and none is made of rock.
2. The Persian Gulf is a smaller, broad inlet of the sea, like the Bay of Bengal.
3. The Bay of Bengal is called the world's largest bay.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: A student says: 'If we save the Great Barrier Reef, we will have saved about one-quarter of all ocean species.' Evaluate the claim using the chapter. Say what the one-quarter figure refers to, what the Great Barrier Reef is, what it houses, and what protects its status.
questions.a: The one-quarter figure is for reefs in general: the chapter says reefs provide food and shelter for about one-quarter of all ocean species. The Great Barrier Reef is one reef, off Australia's northeastern coast, over 2,000 km long. It houses hundreds of species of coral and thousands of species of fish and other animals and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. So the claim overreaches: saving this one reef would not save a quarter of all species, though conserving reefs, including this one, is crucial.
s: The one-quarter figure belongs to reefs in general
The Great Barrier Reef is one reef, location and length
What it houses: coral and fish species
UNESCO World Heritage Site
Verdict: overreaches, but conservation is crucial

questions.q:
A shipping firm in Gujarat compares two harbour sites. Site P is on a smaller, broad inlet of the sea. Site Q is on an open coast facing the full strength of the ocean winds. The firm also needs the shortest sea route for cargo from India to Europe.
(a) What kind of water body is Site P, in the chapter's classification?
(b) Which site does the chapter's reasoning favour for a port and dockyard, and why?
(c) Name the man-made waterway that the chapter calls the shortest maritime route from India to Europe, and say which two water bodies it connects.
(d) The firm's chairman says: 'The Persian Gulf and the Bay of Bengal are both bays.' Correct him using the table's descriptions.
questions.a: (a) A bay, a smaller, broad inlet of the sea. (b) Site P, because bays provide safe havens for ports and dockyards, shielding them from the strong winds of the open oceans. (c) The Suez Canal, connecting the Red Sea with the Mediterranean, opened in 1869. (d) The Bay of Bengal is a bay, a smaller broad inlet, while the Persian Gulf is a gulf, a large inlet of the sea deeply cutting into land.
s: Part (a): a bay
Part (b): Site P; bays shield ports from strong ocean winds
Part (c): the Suez Canal joining the Red Sea and the Mediterranean
Part (d): Bay of Bengal is a bay; Persian Gulf is a gulf

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Great Barrier Reef has just one kind of coral and a few fish.' Correct her using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says the Great Barrier Reef is a complex, interconnected habitat housing hundreds of species of coral and thousands of species of fish and other sea animals.
s: Hundreds of species of coral
Thousands of species of fish and other sea animals

questions.q:
(a) A town's fishing fleet empties the water of fish, its drains carry waste into the sea, and the climate keeps changing. Match each to the chapter's threat to reefs.
(b) Say what the bleaching and death of coral then does to the other animals of the reef.
questions.a: (a) Overfishing, pollution and climate change, in that order. (b) It leads to the loss of habitat of a whole host of sea animals that live in the reef.
s: (a) Overfishing, pollution, climate change
(b) Loss of habitat of many sea animals

questions.q: Write a short situation, in two sentences, in which a port is built on a bay rather than on an open coast, and give the chapter's reason for the choice.
questions.a: For example: a state plans a port and dockyard and picks a bay for them. The chapter says bays provide safe havens for ports and dockyards, shielding them from the strong winds of the open oceans.
s: A situation in which a port is sited on a bay
Reason: safe haven for ports and dockyards
Shielded from the strong winds of the open oceans

questions.q: A coastal state plans a new harbour and wants its ships sheltered from the strong winds of the open ocean. Which kind of water body does the chapter say suits ports and dockyards for this reason?
questions.a: A bay, which gives ports safe havens from wind
o: A bay, which gives ports safe havens from wind
A strait, because a narrow channel is always calm and sheltered from every wind
A canal, because a man-made channel keeps out all the wind from the sea
An open sea, because its large size spreads out the wind and the waves

questions.q: Kiran says: 'The Suez Canal is a natural strait that has joined the Red Sea and the Mediterranean since earliest times, and it is the shortest sea route from India to Europe.' Test each half and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The second half is right: the chapter calls it the shortest maritime route from India to Europe. The first half is wrong: it is a canal, a man-made channel, opened in 1869, not a natural strait.
s: Second half correct: shortest maritime route from India to Europe
First half wrong: man-made canal opened in 1869
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: A shipping company in Gujarat has two needs: a harbour sheltered from strong ocean winds, and the shortest sea route from India to Europe. For each, name the type of water body from the chapter and one named example, and say what the chapter says about the example. Then say what a student should not claim about the first example's kind.
questions.a: For the sheltered harbour the answer is a bay, as in the Bay of Bengal, since bays are safe havens for ports and dockyards shielding them from the strong winds of the open oceans; the Bay of Bengal is the world's largest bay and has been important in trade. For the short route the answer is a canal, the Suez Canal, a human-made passage opened in 1869 that connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean and is the shortest maritime route from India to Europe. A student should not call the Bay of Bengal a gulf or a sea, since a bay is a smaller, broad inlet of the sea.
s: Bay for the sheltered harbour
Why bays shelter ports; Bay of Bengal largest and used in trade
Canal and the Suez Canal as the shortest route
Opened 1869, human-made, joins Red Sea and Mediterranean
A bay is a smaller broad inlet, not a gulf or a sea

questions.q: A student says, 'A canal and a strait are the same thing, since both connect water bodies.' Using the chapter's table, give the difference.
questions.a: A strait is a narrow channel joining two seas or oceans, while a canal is a man-made channel connecting water bodies, so a canal is made by people and a strait is not described as man-made.
s: Strait: narrow channel joining seas or oceans
Canal: man-made channel

questions.q: A student says, 'Calling reefs the rainforests of the sea is just poetry.' Give two facts from the chapter that make the comparison fair, and one example of the animals involved.
questions.a: Reefs are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth, and they provide food and shelter for about one-quarter of all ocean species. Examples are fish, crabs, turtles and sponges.
s: Among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth
Food and shelter for about one-quarter of all ocean species
An example such as fish, crabs, turtles or sponges

questions.q: True or False? 'A fishing cooperative sinks old concrete blocks to build a ridge just below the sea surface. By the chapter's definition this ridge can be called a reef.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter defines a reef as a ridge at or near the surface of the ocean, formed either naturally or artificially, so a ridge built by people can be called a reef.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the definition allows a reef to be formed artificially

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the water body in Column B that the chapter ties to it.
Column A: 1. A cargo from India to Europe takes the shortest maritime route.  2. A port needs a safe haven from the strong winds of the open ocean.  3. A trader notes a route used for trade between India and Europe for millennia.  4. A fisher works the largest bay in the world.
Column B: a. the Suez Canal  b. a bay  c. the Persian Gulf  d. the Bay of Bengal

Assertion (A): Every reef in the ocean is built by corals.
Reason (R): Natural reefs can be made of rock or built by tiny sea animals called corals.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
A diver compares two sections of the same reef, surveying 40 coral colonies in each. In Section A, 38 of the 40 colonies are alive and many fish and crabs shelter among them. In Section B, only 9 of the 40 are alive; the rest are bleached and dead and few animals remain. Tests show that the chemical composition of the water in Section B has changed.
(a) Name the process seen in Section B.
(b) What does the chapter say causes it?
(c) Predict what the loss of the coral does to the animals that used Section B, using the chapter.
(d) The conservation team's rule is to work where the greatest share of surveyed colonies is dead. Which section does the rule pick, and what share is dead there?
questions.a: (a) Coral bleaching. (b) Changes in the chemical composition of ocean waters, largely caused by human actions. (c) Bleaching and death of the coral leads to the loss of habitat of a whole host of sea animals, so the animals that sheltered there lose their home. (d) Section B: 31 of 40 colonies, 77.5 per cent, are dead, against 2 of 40, 5 per cent, in Section A.
s: Part (a): coral bleaching
Part (b): changed ocean-water chemistry, largely from human actions
Part (c): loss of habitat of sea animals
Part (d): Section B, 77.5 per cent dead against 5 per cent

questions.q:
(a) State the Tibetan Plateau's extent from east to west and from north to south.
(b) Using (a), find the area of a rectangle with those sides, and say why the answer is only a rough estimate for the plateau.
questions.a: (a) About 2,500 km east to west and about 1,000 km north to south. (b) 2,500 x 1,000 = 2,500,000 square kilometres. It is rough because the plateau is not a perfect rectangle and both lengths are given as 'about'.
s: (a) 2,500 km and 1,000 km
(b) 2,500,000 sq km, rough because the shape is not a rectangle

questions.q: A student says the Tibetan Plateau is 'nearly square'. Using its two extents from the chapter, show the claim cannot be right.
questions.a: The plateau stretches about 2,500 km from east to west and about 1,000 km from north to south. Its east-west length is 2.5 times its north-south length, so it is far longer one way than the other and cannot be nearly square.
s: The two extents: 2,500 km and 1,000 km
Ratio 2.5 to 1
Conclusion: not nearly square

questions.q: Show that the statement 'every desert is hot, like the Sahara' cannot be true, using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says some deserts are hot, such as the Sahara and the Thar, but others are cold, like the Gobi in Asia. One cold desert is enough to make the statement false.
s: The chapter names hot deserts
It names the Gobi as a cold desert
One counter-example makes the statement false

questions.q: A school atlas lists the continents and a student adds 'the Arctic' as an eighth. Using the chapter's most common count, respond.
questions.a: The most common count is seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. The Arctic is not among them, so the student's eighth continent is not part of that count.
s: The most common count is seven
The Arctic is not in the listed seven

questions.q: A newspaper writes that the Tibetan Plateau is called the 'Third Pole' because it is the coldest place on Earth. What is the chapter's reason for the name?
questions.a: Scientists call it that since it contains the largest reserves of freshwater found anywhere outside the polar regions
o: Scientists call it that since it contains the largest reserves of freshwater found anywhere outside the polar regions
It lies midway between the Arctic and the Antarctic and has the same ice cover as both of them at once
It is the coldest desert on Earth, even colder than the Arctic, so it has earned the name
It is the source of rivers that carry the ice of the poles to the Indian Subcontinent

questions.q: A student plans to cross the plateau from east to west on foot at 100 km a day (an illustrative pace), using the chapter's east-west extent. How many days will it take, and why is the answer only an estimate?
questions.a: 2,500 / 100 = 25 days. It is an estimate because the extent is given as 'about' 2,500 km and the pace is assumed.
s: 25 days
The extent is approximate and the pace assumed

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the landform in Column B that fits the chapter's definitions.
Column A: 1. A hiker climbs from a broad base, up steep slopes, to a narrow summit.  2. A farmer works an extensive flat or gently undulating surface with no large hills or deep valleys.  3. A traveller crosses a large, dry expanse with very little precipitation.  4. A surveyor stands on a flat-topped highland that rises from the land, with some steep sides.
Column B: a. plateau  b. mountain  c. plains  d. desert

(a) What does the chapter say the Tibetan Plateau contains that earns it the name 'Third Pole'?
(b) Using (a), say which other places the chapter compares it with when it names it the 'Third' pole.
questions.a: (a) The largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions. (b) The two polar regions, the places that hold the largest freshwater reserves, so the plateau is the third such store.
s: (a) Largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions
(b) The comparison is with the polar regions

questions.q: A news item says: 'Snow-melt is drying out the lakes of the Tibetan Plateau.' Correct it using the chapter, and say what the chapter links the change to.
questions.a: The chapter says snow-melt has expanded existing lakes and created new ones, not dried them, and it links this to climate change.
s: Lakes have expanded and new ones formed
Linked to climate change

questions.q: A guide tells visitors that the Himalayan range was pushed up by one event and the Tibetan Plateau, lying to its north, was made by a different one. How does the chapter correct her?
questions.a: Collisions of the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates formed the plateau and the Himalayas
o: Collisions of the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates formed the plateau and the Himalayas
The plateau was formed by sediment deposition from the Himalayan rivers and only later became so high
The Himalayas formed first and the plateau is just their eroded base worn down by weather
Volcanic activity under the plateau formed it, while the plate collisions formed only the Himalayas

questions.q:
A magazine article on the 'Third Pole' makes four claims. Claim 1: the plateau lies south of the Himalayan Range. Claim 2: it holds the largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions. Claim 3: the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze all begin there. Claim 4: with climate change, snow-melt has caused its lakes to shrink and disappear.
(a) Which claims are wrong, and what does the chapter say instead?
(b) Which single claim gives the chapter's reason for the name Third Pole?
(c) A student wants to quote the article in a school report. Judge what she can safely quote.
questions.a: (a) Claims 1 and 4 are wrong: the plateau lies north of the Himalayan Range, and snow-melt has expanded existing lakes and created new ones. (b) Claim 2: the freshwater reserves are the reason for the name; the rivers are a separate fact. (c) She can safely quote Claims 2 and 3 only; Claims 1 and 4 contradict the chapter.
s: Part (a): claims 1 and 4 with the corrections
Part (b): claim 2 gives the reason for the name
Part (c): quote claims 2 and 3 only

questions.q: A student's field note describes a landform: 'rises from the surrounding land, has a more or less flat surface, and some of its sides are steep slopes.' Which landform does the chapter's definition match?
questions.a: A plateau, since it rises above its surroundings and is flat on top
o: A plateau, since it rises above its surroundings and is flat on top
A plains area, since plains are extensive and flat and may have steep sides
A mountain, since mountains rise above the land with steep slopes
A desert, since a desert is a large expanse that rises above the land around

questions.q: A fact sheet lists three plateaus with illustrative figures. P: 1,800 km east to west, 700 km north to south, average height 2,100 m. Q: 2,500 km east to west, 1,000 km north to south, average height 4,600 m. R: 3,000 km east to west, 1,200 km north to south, average height 3,900 m. Which one could the chapter's description of the Tibetan Plateau fit?
questions.a: Q, whose extents and height agree with the chapter's figures
o: Q, whose extents and height agree with the chapter's figures
P, since the plateau is the smallest of the three and the others are too large to be it
R, since the largest plateau on Earth must have the greatest east to west extent
None, because the chapter gives no figures for the size or height of the plateau

questions.q:
A research agency plans a survey road across the Tibetan Plateau and costs it at an illustrative Rs 4 lakh per km. It can lay the road either along the plateau's full east-west extent or along its full north-south extent, using the chapter's approximate figures. The agency's budget is Rs 50 crore. (1 crore = 100 lakh.)
(a) What would the east-west road cost, in crore rupees?
(b) What would the north-south road cost, in crore rupees?
(c) Which road can the agency afford?
(d) Name the chapter fact that makes these costs estimates only, not exact.
questions.a: (a) 2,500 km x Rs 4 lakh = Rs 10,000 lakh = Rs 100 crore. (b) 1,000 km x Rs 4 lakh = Rs 4,000 lakh = Rs 40 crore. (c) The north-south road, since Rs 40 crore is within Rs 50 crore and Rs 100 crore is not. (d) The chapter gives both extents as 'about' figures.
s: Part (a): Rs 100 crore
Part (b): Rs 40 crore
Part (c): north-south road
Part (d): the extents are 'about' figures

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Tibetan Plateau is the source of major rivers including the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze.
Reason (R): The Himalayan mountain range lies to the south of the Tibetan Plateau.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about landforms.
1. A plateau rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, with some sides often steep.
2. Plains have an extensive flat or gently undulating surface without large hills or deep valleys.
3. The Thar is a hot desert, while the Gobi is a cold one.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three: 1, 2 and 3
o: All three: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A Class 8 student says, 'The Tibetan Plateau is a remote highland, so it matters only to people who live on it.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: It influences Asia's climate and is the source of rivers such as the Indus
o: It influences Asia's climate and is the source of rivers such as the Indus
It matters to the world only because it is the highest plateau, and nothing flows out from it at all
It feeds only the Indus, because the Brahmaputra and Yangtze rise on the Himalayan slopes instead
It matters mainly as a desert, since rivers there come from rain on the Gobi

questions.q: Using the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau, explain how one event can create two very different landforms. Cover the cause, where each lies, how their shapes differ and the plateau's size.
questions.a: Collisions between the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates formed both the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayan mountain range. The plateau lies north of the Himalayan Range. The Himalayas are mountains, with a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit, while the plateau has a more or less flat surface, rising from the surrounding land. The plateau stretches about 2,500 km east to west and 1,000 km north to south, with an average height of over 4,500 metres. So one cause produced a steep range and a vast, high, flat tableland.
s: Cause: plate collisions formed both
Position: plateau north of the Himalayan Range
Mountains: broad base, steep slopes, narrow summit
Plateau: flat surface rising from the land
Plateau size and height

questions.q: Why should a change in the Tibetan Plateau's snow and lakes concern people who live far from it? Use the chapter's facts on rivers, freshwater, climate and the recent change.
questions.a: The plateau is the source of many major rivers, including the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze, so changes there reach the people the rivers serve. It contains the largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions, which is why it is called the Third Pole. It also plays an important role in influencing the climate of Asia. With climate change, snow-melt has already expanded existing lakes and created new ones, which shows the region is changing. Together these facts show that changes on the plateau reach far beyond it.
s: Source of major rivers
Freshwater reserves, the Third Pole
Influence on the climate of Asia
Snow-melt has expanded lakes and created new ones
Conclusion linking the change to people far away

questions.q: Meena says: 'The Himalayas were pushed up first, and they then raised the Tibetan Plateau.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the plateau is the result of collisions between the Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates, and that these same collisions also led to the formation of the Himalayas. The two have one cause; neither raised the other.
s: Plateau is a result of the plate collisions
The same collisions formed the Himalayas
Verdict: no, one cause for both

questions.q: A visitor says a swamp and a tundra are the same, both being 'wet northern land'. Correct her using the chapter's definitions.
questions.a: A tundra is a treeless, cold plain whose soil stays frozen most of the time, while a swamp is land that is always wet and partly covered with water.
s: Tundra: treeless cold plain, soil frozen most of the time
Swamp: always wet, partly covered with water

questions.q: A visitor to the northern Ural region describes three landscapes. One is a treeless, cold plain whose soil stays frozen most of the time. Another is land that is always wet and partly covered with water. The third is a forest of coniferous trees near the Arctic. Which names does the chapter use, in that order?
questions.a: Tundra, swamp and taiga
o: Tundra, swamp and taiga
Steppe, swamp and taiga
Tundra, oasis and savannah
Swamp, tundra and steppe

questions.q:
(a) A steppe tortoise hibernates for 2 to 5 months of the year, depending on the weather. For how many months of the year is it awake, at the least and at the most?
(b) Where does it spend that hibernation, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) 12 - 5 = 7 months at the least and 12 - 2 = 10 months at the most. (b) In its burrow, which is almost 2 metres deep.
s: (a) 7 to 10 months
(b) In a burrow almost 2 metres deep

questions.q: A student says the Urals are 'just rock and minerals with no life'. Give two facts from the chapter that contradict her.
questions.a: The chapter says the Urals support diverse ecosystems, with coniferous taiga forests in the western and eastern parts and deciduous forests in the south, and animals such as brown bears, wolves, lynx, elk, reindeer and sable.
s: Forests: taiga and deciduous
Animals such as brown bears, wolves, lynx, elk, reindeer and sable

questions.q: Show that the Ural Mountains cannot lie entirely within Europe, using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says the Urals form a natural boundary between Europe and Asia. A boundary lies between two regions, so a range that is the boundary between Europe and Asia cannot be entirely inside Europe.
s: The Urals are the boundary between Europe and Asia
A boundary separates two regions
So they cannot lie entirely within Europe

questions.q: In a very warm summer, part of a northern tundra in the Ural region warms and its frozen soil melts. Which outcome does the chapter lead you to expect?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide and methane held in the soil escape and speed up climate change
o: Carbon dioxide and methane held in the soil escape and speed up climate change
The melted soil absorbs extra carbon dioxide and so slows climate change down
The tundra turns into taiga forest at once and stores more greenhouse gases than before
The soil gives off only water, which falls as rain on the nearby steppes and does no harm

questions.q: The Eurasian Steppes and the permafrost of the northern tundra both deal with greenhouse gases, but in opposite ways. Explain how each does so and what the chapter says happens when the permafrost melts.
questions.a: The Steppes are a global carbon sink: the grassland absorbs carbon from the air and stores it underground, which helps to reduce greenhouse effects over time. The tundra's permafrost, the frozen soil, acts like a giant freezer trapping greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. When global warming melts the permafrost, the stored gases are released and speed up climate change. So the Steppes help to reduce the effect, while melting permafrost makes it worse.
s: Steppes absorb carbon from the air
They store it underground and help reduce greenhouse effects
Permafrost traps carbon dioxide and methane
Melting releases them and speeds up climate change
Contrast: one helps reduce, the other adds when it melts

questions.q: Rahul says: 'The Steppes spread over 8,000 km from west to east, so they are more than three times as long as the Urals, which stretch about 2,500 km.' Test his claim with arithmetic and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes. 8,000 / 2,500 = 3.2, and the Steppes are given as spreading over 8,000 km, so they are more than three times the length of the Urals. The Urals are given as about 2,500 km, so the ratio is approximate but the claim holds.
s: 'Over' 8,000 km keeps the ratio above 3
Verdict: yes

questions.q:
Illustrative data for a school project (not from the book): three weather stations in a dry region record 18 cm, 24 cm and 27 cm of precipitation a year. The class also builds a model of the world with 800 pupils standing for all the people on Earth, and uses a 150 million square km strip to stand for all of the Earth's land.
(a) Which stations are in a desert, using the chapter's limit?
(b) Using the chapter's share of land, how many million square km of the model strip are desert?
(c) Using the chapter's share of people, how many of the 800 pupils stand for people living in deserts?
(d) Deserts hold one-fifth of the land but one-eighth of the people. Compared with the world average, are deserts more or less crowded? Show the ratio.
questions.a: (a) The stations with 18 cm and 24 cm, since both are below 25 cm; 27 cm is not. (b) One-fifth of 150 = 30 million square km. (c) One-eighth of 800 = 100 pupils. (d) Share of people divided by share of land = (1/8) / (1/5) = 0.625, so deserts are less crowded than the world average, at 62.5 per cent of it.
s: Part (a): 18 cm and 24 cm
Part (b): 30 million square km
Part (c): 100 pupils
Part (d): ratio 0.625, less crowded

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the landscape in Column B that the chapter gives it.
Column A: 1. A herder moves her animals seasonally to pastures with underground water, in a land of 8 to 9 sunny months.  2. A flat unforested grassland that absorbs carbon and stores it underground.  3. An ancient range that forms the natural boundary between Europe and Asia.  4. A treeless cold plain whose frozen soil traps greenhouse gases.
Column B: a. the Gobi Desert  b. the Eurasian Steppes  c. the Ural Mountains  d. the tundra
Three weather stations in a dry region record 18 cm, 24 cm and 26 cm of precipitation a year. Using the chapter's limit for deserts, the number of these stations that lie in a desert is ___.
A student says: 'The Gobi is a desert, so it must be hot, like the Sahara.' Correct her using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter names the Gobi as a cold desert, in contrast to hot deserts like the Sahara and the Thar; its winter temperatures can drop to minus 30 degrees Celsius.
s: The Gobi is a cold desert
Winter temperatures can drop to minus 30 degrees Celsius

questions.q: The chapter shows solar panels and windmills in the Gobi Desert. (a) Which feature of Mongolia's weather suits solar panels? (b) What does the chapter's caption say these panels and windmills do?
questions.a: (a) About 8 to 9 months of sunny weather in a year. (b) They harness energy from Nature.
s: (a) 8 to 9 months of sunny weather
(b) Harnessing energy from Nature

questions.q: Write a short situation, in two sentences, about a migratory bird such as the Siberian crane that depends on the Steppes, and say two things the chapter says the Steppes do.
questions.a: For example: a Siberian crane flying across Eurasia rests at a steppe water body before flying on. The chapter says the steppes and nearby water bodies serve as resting spots for migratory birds, and the grassland is a global carbon sink that absorbs carbon and stores it underground.
s: A situation with a migratory bird resting on the steppe
Resting spot for migratory birds
Global carbon sink: absorbs and stores carbon underground

questions.q: A family of herders on the edge of the Gobi Desert plans its year. The land has sparse vegetation and a harsh climate. According to the chapter, what do herds there do to survive?
questions.a: Migrate seasonally to reach pastures that are supported by underground water supplies, as vegetation is sparse
o: Migrate seasonally to reach pastures that are supported by underground water supplies, as vegetation is sparse
Stay in one place all year and rely on the sunny months to grow their grass
Move only to the coast in winter, where the sea gives them the water they need
Wait for heavy monsoon rain on the desert floor before they move their herds on

questions.q: Compare the Gobi Desert and the Eurasian Steppes. Cover their place, climate, vegetation, how life copes, and one way each matters for the world or for people.
questions.a: The Gobi is in Mongolia, with part in north China, and is a cold desert; Mongolia has 8 to 9 months of sunny weather but winter temperatures can fall to minus 30 degrees Celsius. Its vegetation is sparse, and herds migrate seasonally to pastures supported by underground water. The Steppes spread over 8,000 km west to east as flat unforested grassland with a temperate climate, hot summers, cold winters and moderate seasonal rainfall. They are a global carbon sink, absorbing carbon from the air and storing it underground, and they shelter migratory birds such as the Siberian crane. Both support life in demanding climates, the Gobi through herding and the Steppes through grass and birds.
s: Gobi place and cold climate
Gobi sparse vegetation and seasonal herd migration
Steppes grassland and climate
Steppes as carbon sink and bird stop
A comparison point across the two

questions.q:
Read the statements about deserts, the Steppes and mountains.
1. Deserts are found on every continent and cover about one-fifth of the Earth's land area.
2. The Eurasian Steppes spread for over 8,000 km from west to east.
3. Mountains are formed only by erosion and play no role in determining climates.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
All three: 1, 2 and 3
1 only
3 only

questions.q:
A photographer in Mongolia notes that in winter the temperature drops to minus 30 degrees Celsius, yet the country is called the 'Land of the Eternal Blue Sky'. Her herder host says the family's animals move to different pastures through the year. A solar-power firm is choosing between Site X, in the Mongolian Gobi region, and Site Y in a region with only 3 months of sunny weather a year (an illustrative figure).
(a) Explain why the name and the cold winter do not contradict each other.
(b) What allows the herds to find pasture in such a dry land?
(c) Is the Gobi a hot desert or a cold one?
(d) Which site should the firm choose for solar panels, going by the chapter's figure for Mongolia's sunny weather, and why?
questions.a: (a) The name comes from about 8 to 9 months of sunny weather, which is about sunshine, not warmth, so a very cold winter is consistent. (b) Herds migrate seasonally to pastures supported by underground water supplies. (c) A cold desert. (d) Site X: the chapter gives Mongolia about 8 to 9 months of sunny weather, against only 3 at Site Y, so X offers far more sunshine for solar panels.
s: Part (a): name is about sunny months, not temperature
Part (b): seasonal migration to pastures with underground water
Part (c): a cold desert
Part (d): Site X, 8 to 9 sunny months against 3

questions.q: True or False? 'A mountain range can serve as a natural boundary only between countries, so the Ural Mountains cannot be a boundary between two continents.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says mountains, in many cases, serve as natural boundaries between countries, but it also says the Ural Mountains form a natural boundary between Europe and Asia, which are continents.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Urals are a natural boundary between the continents Europe and Asia

questions.q: A mountain range supplies freshwater through melting snow and glaciers, shelters many species and forms a boundary between two countries. Which roles of mountains from the chapter does it show, in that order?
questions.a: Water tower, biodiversity hotspot and natural boundary
o: Water tower, biodiversity hotspot and natural boundary
Climate maker, desert edge and carbon sink
Biodiversity hotspot, water tower and carbon sink
Natural boundary, permafrost store and water tower

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mongolia is called the 'Land of the Eternal Blue Sky'.
Reason (R): Mongolia has about 8 to 9 months of sunny weather in a year.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Grasslands like the Eurasian Steppes only add to the greenhouse effect, because grass gives off carbon.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The steppes absorb carbon from the air and store it underground
o: The steppes absorb carbon from the air and store it underground
The steppes absorb carbon, but they store it above ground in the grass, where it is soon released again
The steppes neither absorb nor give off carbon, since only forests and oceans take part in this
The steppes reduce the greenhouse effect only by shading the land and cooling the air above it

questions.q: A student writes in her notes: 'The edelweiss is a tree of the Alps' lower slopes, where oak and beech forests grow.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The edelweiss is an alpine flower of the high mountains, and the oak and beech forests grow at lower altitudes
o: The edelweiss is an alpine flower of the high mountains, and the oak and beech forests grow at lower altitudes
The edelweiss is a spruce of the higher slopes, above the oak and beech forests
The edelweiss is an alpine flower of the lowlands, below the oak and beech forests
The edelweiss is a tree of the high mountains, where spruce and pine give way to snow

questions.q:
Read the statements about plains, valleys and the Alps.
1. Plains are vast flatlands formed by sediment deposition and known for fertile soils.
2. Valleys are formed by sediment deposition on flat land, not carved by rivers.
3. The European Plain has been the ground for major battles, with many rulers jostling to control it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
All three: 1, 2 and 3
1 only
2 only

questions.q: A student claims that Moscow, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Warsaw grew into major cities because they lie on high mountain passes. What does the chapter say supported the growth of these cities?
questions.a: Relatively flat land and a favourable climate supported their growth
o: Relatively flat land and a favourable climate supported their growth
The mountain minerals of the Alps, which were mined and then traded to each city by river
The battles of the plain, which gave each city rulers who were eager to protect fertile land
The Alps acting as a natural barrier in south-central Europe that kept each of them safe

questions.q: A travel poster says: 'The Alps are covered in pine forest from the valley floor to the peaks.' Correct the poster using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says oak and beech forests grow at lower altitudes, spruce and pine at higher elevations, and alpine flowers such as the edelweiss in the high mountains, so the forest changes with height and is not all pine.
s: Oak and beech at lower altitudes
Spruce and pine higher, alpine flowers on the high mountains

questions.q: A geography teacher shows two photographs: in one, a river has cut a deep channel through a hillside and left a fertile strip beside it; in the other, a broad flat area lies where layers of material settled out over time. Which pairing agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The river-cut channel is a valley and the broad flat area is a plain formed by sediment deposition
o: The river-cut channel is a valley and the broad flat area is a plain formed by sediment deposition
The river-cut channel is a plain and the flat area is a valley formed by sediment deposition
Both are plains, one formed by the river's cutting and one by the river's deposits settling out over time
Both are valleys, since a river is always at work in each and it alone gives both of them their shape

questions.q:
(a) Name two crops the chapter says are widely cultivated on the European Plain.
(b) What does the chapter's photograph caption say about Europe's share of the world's wheat production?
questions.a: (a) Any two of wheat, barley, rye and potatoes. (b) The largest proportion of the world's wheat production is from Europe.
s: (a) Two of wheat, barley, rye, potatoes
(b) Europe has the largest proportion of world wheat production

questions.q: Show that the European Plain cannot be a mountainous region, using the chapter's description of it and its definition of plains.
questions.a: The chapter describes the European Plain as one of the largest flat lands in the world, with low-lying terrain, gentle rolling hills and wide river valleys. Plains are defined as flatlands without large hills or deep valleys, so a plain cannot be mountainous.
s: Described as low-lying flat land with gentle rolling hills
Plains have no large hills
So it cannot be mountainous

questions.q: Trace how the Alps help a farmer in lowland Europe, naming the rivers and three uses the chapter gives.
questions.a: The Alps provide water to major European rivers like the Rhine and the tributaries of the Danube. These rivers supply drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power to lowland Europe, so a lowland farmer can irrigate fields with water that began in the mountains.
s: The Alps provide water to the Rhine and Danube tributaries
Three uses: drinking, irrigation, hydroelectric power
Link to the farmer's irrigation

questions.q:
A student copies five statements about the Alps from a website. 1: They are crescent-shaped. 2: They lie in northern Europe. 3: Oak and beech forests grow at lower altitudes. 4: The range has no minerals. 5: Its water feeds the Rhine and tributaries of the Danube.
(a) Which statements contradict the chapter?
(b) Correct each of them.
(c) Which statement shows that the vegetation changes with height?
(d) A teacher says she may quote statements 1, 3 and 5 in class. Judge this.
questions.a: (a) Statements 2 and 4. (b) The Alps form a natural barrier in south-central Europe, not northern Europe; they are rich in minerals such as iron, copper, lead, rock salt, graphite, gypsum and magnesite. (c) Statement 3: oak and beech at lower altitudes, spruce and pine higher, alpine flowers in the high mountains. (d) The teacher is right: statements 1, 3 and 5 agree with the chapter.
s: Part (a): statements 2 and 4
Part (b): south-central Europe; rich in minerals
Part (c): statement 3, forests by altitude
Part (d): safe to quote 1, 3 and 5

questions.q: Explain why the European Plain has supported dense populations and major cities. Use its soils and crops, its rivers, its mineral deposits, and the land and climate.
questions.a: Its fertile soils make it one of the most productive agricultural regions in the world, growing wheat, barley, rye and potatoes, which feed dense populations. Its rivers have played an important role in trade and transport. Its deposits of coal, oil and natural gas have been important for economic growth. The relatively flat land and favourable climate have supported the growth of major cities such as Moscow, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Warsaw.
s: Fertile soils and crops
Rivers for trade and transport
Coal, oil and natural gas for economic growth
Flat land and favourable climate
Link to major cities and dense populations

questions.q: On a hike up an Alpine slope, a student notes the trees and flowers at three heights. Which order, from the foot of the slope to the high mountain, matches the chapter?
questions.a: Oak and beech, then spruce and pine, then alpine flowers such as the edelweiss in the high mountains
o: Oak and beech, then spruce and pine, then alpine flowers such as the edelweiss in the high mountains
Spruce and pine, then oak and beech, then alpine flowers such as the edelweiss at the top
Alpine flowers such as the edelweiss, then spruce and pine, then oak and beech at the very top of the climb
Oak and beech, then alpine flowers such as the edelweiss, then spruce and pine at the top

questions.q:
(a) How does the chapter say plains and valleys are each formed?
(b) Using (a), explain why a plain beside a river valley suits farming.
questions.a: (a) Plains are formed by sediment deposition; valleys are carved by rivers. (b) Plains have fertile soils that support farming, and a river valley adds fertile soil, water and transport routes, so together they sustain agriculture.
s: (a) Plains by sediment deposition; valleys carved by rivers
(b) Fertile soil plus water and transport routes sustain agriculture

questions.q: A mapmaker labels the Alps 'a straight wall across northern Europe'. Correct two points using the chapter.
questions.a: The Alps are crescent-shaped, not straight, and they form a natural barrier in south-central Europe, not northern Europe.
s: Crescent-shaped, not straight
South-central Europe, not northern

questions.q: Compare the Alps and the European Plain on four points: the shape of the land, what grows or lives there, the minerals they hold, and what they give the people of Europe.
questions.a: The Alps are a crescent-shaped mountain range, whereas the European Plain is low-lying flat land with gentle rolling hills and wide river valleys. The Alps carry oak and beech forests low down, spruce and pine higher up and alpine flowers, with wildlife such as ibex, chamois and golden eagles; the Plain grows wheat, barley, rye and potatoes. The Alps are rich in iron, copper, lead, rock salt and other minerals, and the Plain has coal, oil and natural gas. The Alps give water to rivers like the Rhine for drinking, irrigation and power, and a setting for skiing and hiking, while the Plain gives farming, transport and sites for major cities.
s: Shape of the land
Vegetation, crops and wildlife
Minerals of each
What the Alps give: water and recreation
What the Plain gives: farming, transport and cities

questions.q: A planner chooses a village site in a river valley and lists three benefits the chapter says valleys provide. Which list matches the chapter?
questions.a: Fertile soil, water and transport routes
o: Fertile soil, water and transport routes
Fertile soil, rock salt and a natural barrier against invaders
Skiing, hiking and picturesque landscapes for visitors
Coal, oil and natural gas for economic growth

questions.q:
A planner studies four sites. Site A has a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. Site B is an extensive flat land with gentle rolling hills and wide river valleys. Site C is a flat-topped highland that rises from the land with some steep sides. Site D is a large, dry expanse with very little precipitation. The planner wants a grain depot where farming is strong and rivers can carry goods.
(a) Name the landform at each site.
(b) Which site should get the depot, and why, according to the chapter's account of plains?
(c) What does the chapter say the rivers of the European Plain have done for trade?
(d) Name two resources of the European Plain that the chapter says helped economic growth.
questions.a: (a) A: mountain; B: plains; C: plateau; D: desert. (b) Site B: plains have fertile soils that support farming, trade and dense populations, and wide river valleys give water and transport routes. (c) They have played an important role in trade and transport. (d) Any two of coal, oil and natural gas.
s: Part (a): mountain, plains, plateau, desert
Part (b): Site B, fertile soils and river valleys
Part (c): important role in trade and transport
Part (d): two of coal, oil, natural gas

questions.q: Write a three-line diary of a hiker climbing an Alpine slope, one line at the foot, one midway and one high up, naming the trees or flowers she sees and one animal she might meet.
questions.a: For example: 'At the foot I walk among oak and beech. Higher up, spruce and pine take over. High on the mountain the edelweiss grows, and a golden eagle circles above.' The trees and flowers must follow the chapter's order by altitude and the animal must be one the chapter names for the Alps.
s: Foot: oak and beech
Higher: spruce and pine
High: alpine flowers such as the edelweiss, and an animal the chapter names

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The European Plain has been the ground for major battles.
Reason (R): The European Plain has deposits of coal, oil and natural gas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Neha says: 'Because the European Plain is flat and has fertile soils, farming, trade and dense populations are all to be expected there.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says plains are vast flatlands known for fertile soils that support farming, trade and dense populations, and that the European Plain's fertile soils make it one of the most productive agricultural regions, with rivers important for trade and transport and several major cities.
s: Plains: fertile soils support farming, trade and dense populations
European Plain: productive farming, trade rivers and cities
Verdict: yes

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why major cities grew on the European Plain.
questions.a: The relatively flat land and the favourable climate supported the growth of major cities such as Moscow, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Warsaw.
s: Relatively flat land
Favourable climate

questions.q: A student says, 'Mountains like the Alps have nothing to do with the farms and power stations of lowland Europe.' Which reply is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The Alps give water to the Rhine and to tributaries of the Danube, which supply drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power to lowland Europe
o: The Alps give water to the Rhine and to tributaries of the Danube, which supply drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power to lowland Europe
The Alps shelter the lowlands, but the chapter links their rivers only to forests and wildlife on the slopes and valleys
The Alps supply water to the Rhine, but the Rhine serves only drinking water and not power or irrigation
The Alps do not feed any rivers, but their minerals are carried to lowland factories by train and road

questions.q: A map-reader notes a region of wide open spaces with scattered trees and seasonal rainfall, lying between a tropical rainforest on one side and a desert on the other. Which ecosystem does the chapter describe this as?
questions.a: A savannah, a tropical grassland ecosystem with wide open spaces and scattered trees that lies mainly between rainforests and deserts
o: A savannah, a tropical grassland ecosystem with wide open spaces and scattered trees that lies mainly between rainforests and deserts
A steppe, a flat unforested grassland of temperate climate with hot summers and cold winters
A tundra, a treeless cold plain whose soil stays frozen most of the time and traps gases
